articles.text: 100% of eligible Piedmonters have received dose of vaccine All fully vaccinated city staff members will be welcomed back to the workplace on Tuesday, July 6. A report was provided to councilmembers by Fire Chief Dave Brannigan at a June 21 meeting. Brannigan explained that July 6 was chosen as a tentative “re-opening date” because of the nature of changing Cal/ OSHA regulations, and lack of certainty. The governor, and the California department of Public Health, has lifted most major restrictions regarding COVID. In addition, based on Alameda County’s reported statistics, Piedmont is the first and only city in the county to reach 100% of the available population over the age of 12 to receive their first vaccine, and over 80% are fully vaccinated. “This gives [city staff] a few weeks to make sure our interpretations are accurate, and that employees have the opportunity to adjust their lives,” Brannigan said following the June 21 staff meeting. Re-opening the city would begin with City Hall. Vaccinated members of the public will be allowed into city hall for services. This would be done through an “honor system,” keeping in mind that nearly all residents are now fully vaccinated. articles.text: Editor: As someone who has lived in Piedmont for 15 years, one thing that has been a constant is the 4th of July parade. I can recall being very young and watching the marching bands and the old cars drive by. It was always a source of joy during the summertime for me and many others. As we all know, the parade was cancelled last year due to the pandemic, and I believe that was the best choice. But now things are different. Things are re-opening. And I think that it is safe and possible for us to have a parade. Here’s why: 82.5% of eligible people are fully vaccinated for COVID-19 in Piedmont, the highest rate in Alameda County. Fully vaccinated people are able to be with each other without masks, so this makes the parade much safer than last year. Also, the parade is an outdoor activity. As many of us know, outdoor activities are far safer than indoor activities with regards to COVID-19. But above all other reasons, we as a community need a big activity like this to bring us together again. Over the course of more than a year we have had to adapt to online meetings and social distancing, and it has been extremely tough. We have all had moments of hardship during lockdown, but I think a 4th of July parade would be the perfect thing to lift the community’s spirits. articles.text: A change of school leadership is overdue. Leading in education, especially in this era, requires more than just reacting in crisis mode and apologizing for failures and harm once public recognition demands it. Piedmont Unified School District has received national and local media attention for several scandals involving discriminatory conduct of racial, sexual, and anti-Semitic nature: Football Fantasy Slut League, the Cowherd incident, student dance formations of a swastika, hate speech on lockers, and recently the white support circle. Superintendent Booker’s responses to these incidents have been defensive, lacking in transparency, and have failed to fix the damage to our female and BIPOC students. We have been made to accept and absorb the effects of egregious behavior and dismissive apologies from the city’s highest paid administrator. Even if well meaning, responses that are tone deaf to the needs of minorities and the less privileged protect offenders and discount the victims’ experience. To chastise instead of supporting students of color and female students for bringing up harassment experienced at school has far-reaching, lifelong consequences. articles.text: A report of the 2019 greenhouse gas emissions inventory, and goals accomplished related to Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, was provided to City Council on Monday evening, June 21. The report was produced by Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo. The report found that natural gas and personal transportation are now the primary sources of emissions in Piedmont. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets an ambitious goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. The goal is considered met if the city does not emit more than 29,291 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in a single year. The report garnered information on the city’s GHG emissions through 2019. Compiling data annually allows the city to track its progress toward meeting its climate action plan. The 2019 GHG emissions inventory was completed in spring of this year and shows that Piedmont’s emissions were approximately 34,197 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents. This shows a large reduction of 30% below 2005 levels, but a slight reduction of less than 1% from the year before, 2018. The large reductions in 2005 can be attributed to decreases in emissions from building appliances, Dykman explained. “To achieve these reductions, it is critical to understand the main contributors to emissions,” she said. “The two main contributors (to GHG) in Piedmont have been, and continue to be, residential energy and transportation.” Dykman added that, if Piedmont residents do not reduce emissions from gas vehicles and natural gas use, the city will not meet its CAP goals. “Together, these two sources account for nearly 90% of greenhouse gas emissions,” Dykman said. Redinbo noted that although there was a 30% reduction in emissions between 2005 and 2019, there has been “less than 1% of a reduction in emissions since 2018.” “The main thing to take away from that [statistic] is that residential activities and buildings emit an overwhelming majority of Piedmont’s emissions. While reducing all emissions is important, spending more of our attention on our residential actions will have a larger impact,” he said. Redinbo noted that Piedmont is close to meeting its 2030 emissions goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels, but at this current pace, the city will not meet the 2050 goal without significant changes, mostly in the residential sector. What’s next? The city programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include newly implemented reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free and provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying your kitchen. “Actions considered to be the low-hanging fruit have already been taken, further action is needed in order for the city to be on track in meeting its CAP goals. It will require ongoing commitment that builds upon, and surpasses, the city’s past successes,” Dykman told city councilmembers. The city staff recommended that city council consider a permanent funding source for electrification incentives for homeowners. This includes reducing building permit fees for installation of photovoltaic systems, heat pump water heaters, and heat pump furnaces. The city can also pursue increases in gas user taxes or establish a carbon tax on natural gas. The staff also recommend the creation of a climate action committee, and to create a resolution committing Piedmont’s municipal facilities and activites to be zero-carbon by 2050.
articles.title: Natural gas, vehicles are primary sources of emissions in Piedmont

articles.text: According to Alameda County Public Health Department data, 100 percent of eligible Piedmonters have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, June 20. The news comes days after California widely reopened its economy on Tuesday, June 15 after 15 months of pandemic restrictions. High levels of vaccination are a key part of the state government’s strategy going forward – Gov. Gavin Newsom announced yesterday, Tuesday, June 22 that over 70 percent of Californians ages 12 and older are at least partially vaccinated. However, there are new fears about COVID-19 variants spreading amongst the unvaccinated – on Thursday, June 17, California declared the so-called Delta variant of the COVID-19 virus a “variant of concern.” There have only been several hundred of positive cases of the Delta reported in California, but the rates have been increasing week-over-week, troubling officials. Low positivity and high vaccination rates have led to even more restrictions being eliminated in recent days. Late last week, state workplace safety agency Cal/OSHA revised rules so that fully vaccinated workers can forego masks indoors. Previous to the rule change, Cal/OSHA had declared workers must wear masks inside unless everyone in a room was fully vaccinated. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. Starting last week, social distancing and capacity limits were lifted statewide. Fully vaccinated can go without masks in almost all situations, but unvaccinated people are still required to wear masks indoors. Some exemptions to the updated mask mandate exist. All people must still wear masks while in public transit, airplanes, transit hubs, schools, healthcare facilities, prisons and homeless shelters. While the number of vaccinations administered in Alameda County have dipped in recent days, almost 2 million jabs have been injected into arms countywide as of this week. articles.text: At its meeting on June 21, the Piedmont City Council delayed final approval of the installation of electric vehicle (EV) charging station in the center of town. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) and city staff have worked together to plan the installation of EV charging stations and proposed locations by the Piedmont tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. A 10-year agreement would allow EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. The stations would be maintained and operated by EBCE at no cost to the city. CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo called the proposal a “win-win” for the city in terms of reaching its ambitious Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Jessie Denver, a representative of East Bay Community Energy at the meeting, confirmed that Bonita Avenue was the most desirable location because it is adjacent to commercial retail, and that a one-hour charging limit and 24-hour accessibility would encourage turnover. “We want those chargers to be highly utilized, and turnover to happen rapidly,” Denver said, and added that there seemed to be “ample parking space in the Civic Center area” of Piedmont, adjacent to the tennis courts. Mayor Teddy Gray King disagreed, noting that the area is “next to city hall, a high school, middle school, and lots of residences. To suggest it’s easy to find parking [there] is just never the case,” she said. Councilmembers agreed that having EV charging stations in the city would be ideal but discussed other locations and configurations. They also noted that a one-hour turnaround is not ideal in that location, where educators, school, and Recreation Department employees often park. City Planner Kevin Jackson confirmed that other potential locations are being considered. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit, acting as city administrator in interim, suggested to delay the vote with EBCE until other options are explored. He noted that it could return to city council in a month. “This is a 10-year contract. We’d like to better understand the flexibility of both parties built in to the contract,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen said. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, June 23, 2021 3 Climate Action Plan successes noted by Council Natural gas, vehicles are primary sources of emissions in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey A report of the 2019 greenhouse gas emissions inventory, and goals accomplished related to Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, was provided to City Council on Monday evening, June 21. The report was produced by Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo. The report found that natural gas and personal transportation are now the primary sources of emissions in Piedmont. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets an ambitious goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. The goal is considered met if the city does not emit more than 29,291 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in a single year. The report garnered information on the city’s GHG emissions through 2019. Compiling data annually allows the city to track its progress toward meeting its climate action plan. The 2019 GHG emissions inventory was completed in spring of this year and shows that Piedmont’s emissions were approximately 34,197 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents. This shows a large reduction of 30% below 2005 levels, but a slight reduction of less than 1% from the year before, 2018. The large reductions in 2005 can be attributed to decreases in emissions from building appliances, Dykman explained. “To achieve these reductions, it is critical to understand the main contributors to emissions,” she said. “The two main contributors (to GHG) in Piedmont have been, and continue to be, residential energy and transportation.” Dykman added that, if Piedmont residents do not reduce emissions from gas vehicles and natural gas use, the city will not meet its CAP goals. “Together, these two sources account for nearly 90% of greenhouse gas emissions,” Dykman said. Redinbo noted that although there was a 30% reduction in emissions between 2005 and 2019, there has been “less than 1% of a reduction in emissions since 2018.” “The main thing to take away from that [statistic] is that residential activities and buildings emit an overwhelming majority of Piedmont’s emissions. While reducing all emissions is important, spending more of our attention on our residential actions will have a larger impact,” he said. Redinbo noted that Piedmont is close to meeting its 2030 emissions goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels, but at this current pace, the city will not meet the 2050 goal without significant changes, mostly in the residential sector. What’s next? The city programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include newly implemented reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free and provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying your kitchen. “Actions considered to be the low-hanging fruit have already been taken, further action is needed in order for the city to be on track in meeting its CAP goals. It will require ongoing commitment that builds upon, and surpasses, the city’s past successes,” Dykman told city councilmembers. The city staff recommended that city council consider a permanent funding source for electrification incentives for homeowners. This includes reducing building permit fees for installation of photovoltaic systems, heat pump water heaters, and heat pump furnaces. The city can also pursue increases in gas user taxes or establish a carbon tax on natural gas. The staff also recommend the creation of a climate action committee, and to create a resolution committing Piedmont’s municipal facilities and activites to be zero-carbon by 2050. City Council holds off on EV charging stations By Allyson Aleksey At its meeting on June 21, the Piedmont City Council delayed final approval of the installation of electric vehicle (EV) charging station in the center of town. East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) and city staff have worked together to plan the installation of EV charging stations and proposed locations by the Piedmont tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. A 10-year agreement would allow EBCE to install two dual-port, fast-charging stations at the location, which would be able to charge up to four vehicles at one time. The stations would be maintained and operated by EBCE at no cost to the city. CivicSpark Fellow Nate Redinbo called the proposal a “win-win” for the city in terms of reaching its ambitious Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Jessie Denver, a representative of East Bay Community Energy at the meeting, confirmed that Bonita Avenue was the most desirable location because it is adjacent to commercial retail, and that a one-hour charging limit and 24-hour accessibility would encourage turnover. “We want those chargers to be highly utilized, and turnover to happen rapidly,” Denver said, and added that there seemed to be “ample parking space in the Civic Center area” of Piedmont, adjacent to the tennis courts. Mayor Teddy Gray King disagreed, noting that the area is “next to city hall, a high school, middle school, and lots of residences. To suggest it’s easy to find parking [there] is just never the case,” she said. Councilmembers agreed that having EV charging stations in the city would be ideal but discussed other locations and configurations. They also noted that a one-hour turnaround is not ideal in that location, where educators, school, and Recreation Department employees often park. City Planner Kevin Jackson confirmed that other potential locations are being considered. Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit, acting as city administrator in interim, suggested to delay the vote with EBCE until other options are explored. He noted that it could return to city council in a month. “This is a 10-year contract. We’d like to better understand the flexibility of both parties built in to the contract,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen said. The news comes days after California widely reopened its economy on Tuesday, June 15 after 15 months of pandemic restrictions. High levels of vaccination are a key part of the state government’s strategy going forward – Gov. Gavin Newsom announced yesterday, Tuesday, June 22 that over 70 percent of Californians ages 12 and older are at least partially vaccinated. However, there are new fears about COVID-19 variants spreading amongst the unvaccinated – on Thursday, June 17, California declared the so-called Delta variant of the COVID-19 virus a “variant of concern.” There have only been several hundred of positive cases of the Delta reported in California, but the rates have been increasing week-over-week, troubling officials. Late last week, state workplace safety agency Cal/OSHA revised rules so that fully vaccinated workers can forego masks indoors. Previous to the rule change, Cal/OSHA had declared workers must wear masks inside unless everyone in a room was fully vaccinated. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. Starting last week, social distancing and capacity limits were lifted statewide. Fully vaccinated can go without masks in almost all situations, but unvaccinated people are still required to wear masks indoors. Some exemptions to the updated mask mandate exist. All people must still wear masks while in public transit, airplanes, transit hubs, schools, healthcare facilities, prisons and homeless shelters. While the number of vaccinations administered in Alameda County have dipped in recent days, almost 2 million jabs have been injected into arms countywide as of this week. articles.text: On Saturday morning, June 19, a group of Piedmonters installed another “Flower Flash” in the city, this time in honor of Pride month. The idea was conceptualized by Piedmont High School sophomore Eve Tellegen, and was made possible with help from members of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Public Works Department, and other city staff. Mini, colorful floral arrangements appeared in two of the city’s most recognizable venues – City Hall and the Exedra – as well as Blair Park, Dracena Park, the Recreation Center, and Highland Avenue in front of the Community Hall. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap and Pam McBain propped up bouquets against the Exedra with red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple bamboo, representing colors on the LGBTQ+ pride flag, which also flies in front of public buildings throughout Piedmont. The two also arranged a caper of flowers with matching vases at City Hall. Gayle Lambert, Lili Bassett, and Molly Ashford designed an arrangement in Dracena Park and in front of the Community Center, and Tellegen, with help from family members and friends, displayed a vivid bouquet at the Recreation Center. The arrangements were on display through Monday, June 21. Former City Administrator Paul Benoit and Assistant City Clerk Lisa Argue. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunalp (left) with Pam McBain

The night before beginning their rafting trip, Troop 15 Scouts enjoy time with each other around a campfire. On the weekend of June 12-13, a group of 56 Piedmont Scouts and parents from Troop 15 rafted 26 miles on the South Fork of the American River. Scouts had an awesome time rafting across raging river rapids and even swimming in the river. In some parts of the river the Scouts could leap out of their rafts to be carried down the river a brief way by the currents. For regular rapids, Scouts paddled down the water, maneuvering around rocks, with their paddles in sync. The weekend on the water was exciting and a new experience for many of the younger Scouts. “Our entire patrol attended, all 10 of us,” said Caleb Canada. “Nobody wanted to miss this trip. All of us had a fantastic time rafting down the river. We were constantly laughing and enjoying ourselves. Everyone agreed that it was an awesome trip.” Scouts also got to admire the beautiful surroundings of the river. The hills, trees, and fields of green and yellow complemented the dark waters of the American River. The guides on the raft helped ensure that the Scouts had fun by adding unique twists to the journey. One raft guide had her entire raft paddle against each other, so their raft spun around in circles as they went down one section of the river. articles.text: Matt Herrick, a Piedmont native (PHS class of 2009), recently received his Master of Business Administration from the University of San Francisco. After attending the University of Southern California for his undergraduate degree, Matt has forged a career as a Product Management leader in the video game industry, working for companies such as PlayStation and most recently Electronic Arts. Locally, he was a valued paperboy with the Piedmont Post in middle school and became a sports writer during high school. “The Piedmont Post has always been a special paper to me,” explained Herrick. “Back in 2003, Gray graciously hired me to be an associate writer, focusing on soccer and then baseball by the end of high school. It was an incredibly rewarding experience, and I am so grateful to have had it growing up. Gray was a kind and patient boss, even when I missed a deadline (I only missed one, I swear). Matt Herrick proudly wears the green graduation sash upon earning an MBA degree from the University of San Francisco. “Thank you for taking a chance on this 12-year-old, Gray,” he said.

articles.text: There is an art to listening. For parents, an important challenge right now is to teach our children how to listen. As our country tunes into the pain caused by generations of social injustice and brutality, our children need to understand what it means to listen, to truly listen. Each year, in my psychology class, I teach students about listening. To begin, I pair them up and give them a simple task: listen to your partner talk about something that’s troubling them, for one minute, without interruption, and then trade places. Invariably, this exercise causes a lot of discomfort. Sure, it can be hard to hear about another person’s troubles, but the discomfort arises mostly because students don’t understand what listening is all about. They don’t know how to simply focus on someone else’s experience, full stop, without inserting themselves into it. Most students are inclined to jump in and problem solve, or share their own experience as a way to connect, but these tactics serve to circumvent the listening process, not to advance it. Also, many students don’t realize that listening takes practice and some feel guilty or embarrassed that they don’t know how to do it well right away. I explain to them that if they want to be good listeners, they need to exercise their listening muscles, so to speak, and there are some basic guidelines that can help. articles.text: Hillary Crissinger was the Director of Special Education for PUSD for the last three years. She will retire on June 30. A total of 11 teachers and staff in Piedmont School District’s Special Education Department have either retired, resigned or requested a leave of absence after the 2020-2021 school year. The list of departures includes Director of Special Education and Student Services Hillary Crissinger and 18 year veteran Occupational Therapist Kimberly Bonacum, both of whom are retiring. Superintendent Randy Booker gave accolades to the retiring Crissinger at the June 9 school board meeting for her three years of service in the district. “Hillary Crissinger is authentic, honest and unbelievably knowledgeable in her field,” Booker said. “It has just been great to be a part of this community,” Crissinger said. “I truly feel like I was contributing in a really positive way to the community and to Special Ed. I had the honor of working with a really solid team that takes a thoughtful and caring approach.” Crissinger spearheaded the Counselor Enrich program in the Special Education Department. In explaining her impact, Booker said, “Hillary brought together all the resources and did all the research through SELPA to help our students in need stay here on campus and have an alternative program. The Counselor Enrich program is [her] legacy.” After adapting to teach Special Education digitally last year, at least 11 positions in the department have been vacated. By Susan Eva Porter, Ph.D. For parents, an important challenge right now is to teach our children how to listen. As our country tunes into the pain caused by generations of social injustice and brutality, our children need to understand what it means to listen, to truly listen. Each year, in my psychology class, I teach students about listening. To begin, I pair them up and give them a simple task: listen to your partner talk about something that’s troubling them, for one minute, without interruption, and then trade places. Invariably, this exercise causes a lot of discomfort. Sure, it can be hard to hear about another person’s troubles, but the discomfort arises mostly because students don’t understand what listening is all about. They don’t know how to simply focus on someone else’s experience, full stop, without inserting themselves into it. Most students are inclined to jump in and problem solve, or share their own experience as a way to connect, but these tactics serve to circumvent the listening process, not to advance it. Also, many students don’t realize that listening takes practice and some feel guilty or embarrassed that they don’t know how to do it well right away. I explain to them that if they want to be good listeners, they need to exercise their listening muscles, so to speak, and there are some basic guidelines that can help. To be an effective listener, begin with the following assumptions: • The person you’re listening to has something important to say. • That something is not about you (even if the topic is about you, the person you’re listening to is sharing their experience, which is different than • • yours, and therefore it’s not really about you). It is not your job to fix the situation, at least not while you’re listening. Doing nothing is doing something. This last assumption can be tough for students to swallow. In almost every other area of their lives they are taught to act, to do something, but when it comes to listening, doing nothing is doing something. In fact, it’s doing a lot. Then I instruct my students to do the following, once their partner has finished speaking: • Thank them for sharing. • Ask relevant follow up questions, if you have them. • Ask if there’s anything you can do to help. • Listen some more. The best way to help children develop good listening skills is to practice them yourself. Take time to listen to your child, parenting partner, family and friends and watch your relationships deepen and transform. It’s what the world needs right now. Not pictured: Quincy Dong A record 28 walkers showed up last Wednesday for the weekly outing of the Piedmont Recreation department-sponsored Walking on Wednesdays group. On hand were Albert Chen, Swee Ling Chen, Jim Kuo, Harriette Louie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Alicia Rivera, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Sherry Jacobs, Larry Olsen, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Haybert Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Pat Mc Swain, Susan Martin, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome first time walkers Stella Houston, Emma Sangil, and Fia Hsu. Drawing from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles, the walkers learned more about early Piedmont developer Frank C. Havens. Havens created and opened the Piedmont Park with its mineral springs attraction in 1898 to promote his land sales. Havens also built a new Piedmont Springs Clubhouse in 1898 at the top of the park across from today’s Wells Fargo bank. The clubhouse overlooked a wooden ravine. Additionally, Havens built a landscaped Maze in 1904 in the current location of Witter Field. A Japanese Tea House was installed in 1907 at its current location in Piedmont Park, and an art gallery at the site of the Park Tennis Courts. He also added a bandstand for Sunday concerts, with rustic park benches, and exotic plants. Havens was a major developer, but around 1915 he experienced financial difficulties. The Oakland Tribune reported that lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against him. Havens auctioned his art collection, and by 1916 he was planning on developing the park into residential home sites to raise money. A mortgage on his Piedmont Park of $172,000 had not been paid and the park was to be sold at a foreclosure action in 1917. The Piedmont School Board wanted 13 acres of the park land for a new high school, but Havens would not sell less than its total 27 acres. The land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to buy 14 acres for a city park, if the City would reimburse them. The School District could also buy the 13 acres it wanted. One year later in 1921 the voters passed a bond issue, and the City reimbursed Alexander and his partners. Prior to this Havens built a large home for himself. His estate, which he called “Wildwood,” was on land that today is the Wildwood Gardens neighborhood. His mansion is the current residence at 101 Wildwood Gardens. Havens initially lived in a house at 801 Magnolia which was built by the Wetmore family for their daughter. The house was later converted to the Christian Science Church and Reading Room, and now is the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The location was convenient for Havens while developing Piedmont Park. He later moved to the Randall house at the corner of Highland and Hazel, which was closer to the construction of his Wildwood estate. The Randall house was originally Miss Ransom’s School for Girls and was demolished around 1930. In 1908 Havens hired Bernard Maybeck to design his grand mansion. It was five stories tall and was stepped down the canyon. It took two years to build and more years to finish the interior. articles.text: Newly renovated sculpture garden unveiled on opening weekend The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) reopened on Friday, June 18, after a 15-month closure. The highlight of the museum’s reopening is its renovated seven-acre campus, including a new entrance from Lake Merritt and redesigned gardens. The museum opened its first weekend to press and museum members. After a seven-month closure, these groups caught the first glimpse of a re-landscaped garden complete with native trees and plantings. A new stage by the main lawn will be used for outdoor programs and performances. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the project design. Renovations were funded by the “All In! The Campaign for OMCA,” which was undertaken to expand OMCA’s role in the community as a public gathering place. To date, $15 million of the overall $85 million campaign was earmarked specifically toward campus and garden renovations. “We are thrilled to finally be reopening and to welcome back the community that has done so much to help sustain us during this challenging time,” said Museum Director Lori Fogarty. “We’re excited to share the updates that have taken place on campus during the closure, which have enhanced the Museum’s role as a public gathering place by creating new spaces for the community to convene.” Oakland-based visual artist Binta Ayofemi designed the new picnic tables, benches, and counters installed throughout the gardens. articles.text: Bobi Cespedes kicks off this year’s Yerba Buena Gardens Festival with a concert on Friday, June 26. The Yerba Buena Gardens Festival returns this summer, kicking off this Friday, June 26. Live music and performance is free to the public. The festival runs through August 28. For more than two decades Yerba Buena Gardens Festival has presented free outdoor music, circus, dance, poetry, theatre, and youth programs by artists from the Bay Area and around the world. The festival was not held last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The festival kicks off this year with a June 26 concert by Bobi Cespedes, the “matriarch of Cuban roots in the Bay Area.” July highlights include the first of a three-part series of dance events by the Yerba Buena Gardens ChoreoFest, music by Zydeco musician Andre Thierry, and Oakland-based hip-hop orchestra Ensemble Mik Nawooj. Children’s programs in July include Pi Clowns and Red Panda Acrobats. “I could not be more thrilled to announce this special Festival season of free performances and concerts this summer,” said Festival Artistic Director Linda Lucero. “I am excited to welcome everyone back to the beautiful Gardens to experience our region’s rich cultural diversity and the immense fortitude of our local artists and performers after a long period of isolation. Yerba Buena Gardens Festival remains a space for art and joy, welcoming people from all walks of life.” Yerba Buena Gardens is located on Mission Street between 3rd and 4th streets in San Francisco. Visit www.ybgfestival.org for a full schedule.

articles.text: Pianist Jeremy Denk’s spring performance in Berkeley is now streaming through July 14 as part of Cal Performances’ “At Home” digital season. Denk has also written about Bach as a great humanist, and described how the composer’s music represents an “intoxicating combination of the divine balanced with the earthy beauty of Pianist Jeremy Denk logic and discipline.” Visit https://secure.calperformances.org/15177/15818 to obtain streaming access. Tickets purchased for each digital event are limited to the account holder. The mission of Cal Performances, part of UC Berkeley, is to produce and present performances of high artistic quality that explore intersections of education and performance art. The Cal Performances “At Home” series makes digital performances available during shelterin-place restrictions.

It was declared the official day when states could allow public gatherings after more than a year of restrictions due to the COVID pandemic. The implications (ramifications, if you will) cause the mind to race. What was will be again. The checkered flag is poised at the starting gate. But will imagination take flight? It depends on how you interpret it. The word “flight” is the key. Many of us were fortunate to have grown up in the heyday of radio. There were live concerts of all sorts. News was presented at the top of the hour; if at all, and only briefly. Radio was the dominion of imagination. Many popular radio programs were devoted to drama and comedy. If you were John Alden Carpenter, you might start out with “Adventures in a perambulator.” Cartoons were drawn by hand by imaginative artists. And then the producer came in and selected the music that was most appropriate to enhance the story. Composers and arrangers created music performed by brilliant Hollywood orchestras. It was live, and it was exciting. The compositions were really inspired. Beethoven enjoyed nature so he wrote his Pastoral Symphony. The storm sequence had an effect on Rossini, and that music was used as the theme for the Lone Ranger series of radio shows. And then Rossini parodied life and inheritance with his Little Pleasure Train. Space travel was not neglected, because there were trips to the moon. And there was music of the spheres long before men walked on the moon. My neighbor Ferde Grofe composed the pictorial Grand Canyon Suite and the Mississippi Suite. The music told you everything. You didn’t even need to be there. That was – and is – the miracle of imagination. Composers of genius continue to write pieces for flights of imagination. articles.text: If you don’t have a spouse or children, you might think you don’t need to do much estate planning. But if you have any assets, any familial connections, any interest in supporting charitable groups – not to mention a desire to control your own future – you do need to establish an estate plan. In evaluating your needs for this type of planning, let’s start with what might happen if you die intestate – that is, without a last will and testament. In this scenario, your assets will likely have to go through the probate process, which means they’ll be distributed by the court according to your state’s intestate succession laws, essentially without regard to your wishes. Even if you don’t have children yourself, you may have nephews or nieces, or even children of cousins or friends, to whom you would like to leave some of your assets, which can include not just money but also cars, collectibles, family memorabilia and so on. But if everything you own goes through probate, there’s no guarantee that these individuals will end up with what you wanted them to have. If you want to leave something to family members or close friends, you will need to indicate this in your last will and testament or other estate planning documents. But you also may want to provide support to one or more charitable organizations. Of course, you can simply name these charities in your will, but there may be options that could provide you with more benefits. One such possibility is a charitable remainder trust. Under this arrangement, you’d transfer appreciated assets – such as stocks, mutual funds or other securities – into an irrevocable trust. The trustee, whom you’ve named – in fact, you could serve as trustee yourself – can then sell the assets at full market value, avoiding the capital gains taxes you’d have to pay if you sold them yourself, outside a trust. Plus, if you itemize, you may be able to claim a charitable deduction on your taxes. With the proceeds, the trust can purchase income-producing assets and provide you with an income stream for the rest of your life. Upon your death, the remaining trust assets will go the charities you’ve named. Aside from family members and charitable groups, there’s a third entity that’s central to your estate plans: yourself. Everyone should make arrangements to protect their interests, but, in the absence of an immediate family, you need to be especially vigilant about your financial and health care decisions. And that’s why, as part of your estate planning, you may want to include these two documents: durable power of attorney and a health care proxy. A durable power of attorney lets you name someone to manage your finances should you become incapacitated. This arrangement is especially important for anyone who doesn’t have a spouse to step in. And if you become incapacitated, your health care proxy – also known as a health care surrogate or medical power of attorney – lets you name another person to legally make health care decisions for you if you can’t do so yourself. Estate planning moves can be complex, so you’ll need help from a legal professional and possibly your tax and financial advisors. You may not have an immediate family, but you still need to take steps to protect your legacy. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Even “singles” need estate plans If you don’t have a spouse or children, you might think you don’t need to do much estate planning. But if you have any assets, any familial connections, any interest in supporting charitable groups – not to mention a desire to control your own future – you do need to establish an estate plan. In evaluating your needs for this type of planning, let’s start with what might happen if you die intestate – that is, without a last will and testament. In this scenario, your assets will likely have to go through the probate process, which means they’ll be distributed by the court according to your state’s intestate succession laws, essentially without regard to your wishes. Even if you don’t have children yourself, you may have nephews or nieces, or even children of cousins or friends, to whom you would like to leave some of your assets, which can include not just money but also cars, collectibles, family memorabilia and so on. But if everything you own goes through probate, there’s no guarantee that these individuals will end up with what you wanted them to have. If you want to leave something to family members or close friends, you will need to indicate this in your last will and testament or other estate planning documents. But you also may want to provide support to one or more charitable organizations. Of course, you can simply name these charities in your will, but there may be options that could provide you with more benefits. One such possibility is a charitable remainder trust. Under this arrangement, you’d transfer appreciated assets – such as stocks, mutual funds or other securities – into an irrevocable trust. The trustee, whom you’ve named – in fact, you could serve as trustee yourself – can then sell the assets at full market value, avoiding the capital gains taxes you’d have to pay if you sold them yourself, outside a trust. Plus, if you itemize, you may be able to claim a charitable deduction on your taxes. With the proceeds, the trust can purchase income-producing assets and provide you with an income stream for the rest of your life. Upon your death, the remaining trust assets will go the charities you’ve named. Aside from family members and charitable groups, there’s a third entity that’s central to your estate plans: yourself. Everyone should make arrangements to protect their interests, but, in the absence of an immediate family, you need to be especially vigilant about your financial and health care decisions. And that’s why, as part of your estate planning, you may want to include these two documents: durable power of attorney and a health care proxy. A durable power of attorney lets you name someone to manage your finances should you become incapacitated. This arrangement is especially important for anyone who doesn’t have a spouse to step in. And if you become incapacitated, your health care proxy – also known as a health care surrogate or medical power of attorney – lets you name another person to legally make health care decisions for you if you can’t do so yourself. Estate planning moves can be complex, so you’ll need help from a legal professional and possibly your tax and financial advisors. You may not have an immediate family, but you still need to take steps to protect your legacy. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Preheat a grill or grill pan over low heat. 2. Peel the eggplants, then rub the beef and eggplants all over with the sunflower oil and salt, until they are well and evenly coated. 3. Cook the eggplants slowly, about 5 minutes per side for the thinner japanese eggplants, and 10 minutes per side for the plumper globe eggplants, until they are covered in grill marks and tender but not mushy. Remove the eggplants from the grill and allow them to cool slightly. 4. Raise the heat under the grill to high. Sear the steak for about 1 minute on all sides, keeping it rare in the center. Remove from heat and allow to cool slightly. 5. Place the eggplants and steak in a large lidded bowl (or two) which just fits them, and add the marinade. Marinate for at least 12 hours and up to 24 hours, rotating the eggplants and steak so they marinate evenly. 6. A few hours before serving, prepare the crunchy vegetables and the dipping sauce (for the dipping sauce, whisk all of the ingredients together until well-combined). 7. Remove the eggplant and steak from the marinade. Use a sharp knife to slice them very thinly lengthwise on the diagonal (you can also freeze the beef for an hour or so to make it easier to slice thinly). articles.text: Susan Miller-Davis Could what we eat be part of the solution to a more sustainable future? The answer is a resounding “yes!” The cultivation and transport of food causes one third of global emissions, and half of all habitable land is currently being used to produce food. In the US, about 80% of all drinkable water is used for agriculture. As both populations and incomes rise around the world, climate-warming emissions are also growing. Animal products have a higher carbon impact than grains, pulses, vegetables and fruits. Beef, lamb and dairy have the highest carbon impacts of all, for two reasons: ruminants like cattle and sheep create large amounts of methane (a potent greenhouse gas) from their digestive systems; they also require large amounts of grazing and cropland, which contributes significantly to global deforestation. While the connection between fossil fuel extraction and emissions can be clear, the effect our diet has on the environment can be more difficult to see. Compared to even 10 years ago, attitudes about diet have shifted in the U.S. More and more people are embracing “flexitarianism”, eating more vegetables and less red meat, or going even further to adopt vegetarian or vegan diets. More plant-based food products are appearing on shelves and restaurant menus all the time. Despite this, we collectively have a long way to go, and systemic changes matter as much as personal ones. Right now, the federal government encourages meat consumption, giving over $35 billion in subsidies to meat and dairy producers annually, compared with less than 0.5% of that to fruit and vegetable production subsidies. Prices and affordability matter a lot. Large-scale food system change will be needed to make sustainable diets accessible and desirable. That said, change can happen right in our homes, right now. Here are two examples of the change. Susan: the omnivore I work at the intersection of food and climate. My two current projects are conducting research on food waste and plant-rich diets for Project Drawdown and co-authoring a climate-friendly cookbook. I want to help recontextualize how people think about “sustainable” diets, ones that are good for our health and the health of the planet. Spoiler alert: they don’t have to be vegan. Practically speaking, many of us love the flavor of meat, and many of our food traditions and rituals involve meat, from burgers on the grill to a Sunday roast chicken. Animal products also provide important nutrients and minerals that can be harder to come by in vegan diets. For subsistence farmers in many parts of the developing world, livestock provides an important source of income and food security, converting non-arable land into valuable protein and calories. Model diets that can nourish an expected global population of 10 billion people in 2050, lower diet-related disease and mortality, and reduce environmental impacts, all at the same time are being developed by groups like the EAT-Lancet Commission. These diets boil down to balancing calories from a range of foods, and reducing the amount of animal products we consume in affluent countries like the US. So, for example, what does the EAT-Lancet diet look like for a beef-lover? Sticking to about two juicy burgers or a single 14-ounce rib-eye per month. Yup, per month. But there are more creative ways to enjoy beef more often, like this recipe I created which uses beef sparingly but to great effect. You could enjoy a dish like this, which really allows the beef flavor to shine, as often as twice per week without a hint of climate guilt. The Japanese preparation known as tataki flips the conventional marinate-then-cook equation on its head, creating an ultimate make-ahead dish. Serve the flavorful slices of tender beef and silky eggplant at room temperature, to wrap around fresh shredded vegetables and dunk in a savory dipping sauce...it’s a hands-on yet elegant meal to share with friends for a foray back into summer entertaining as California opens up. Nate: the vegan I initially made the switch to a plant-based diet as an environmental decision. Red meat, poultry, and fishing have significant environmental impacts, and changing my diet seemed like a small way to make the world a better place. However, food is complicated. Our personal choices take place against the larger backdrop of our food system and food economy, which undoubtedly will need to shift as well in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Fixing the larger, systemic issues that plague our food economy will require large-scale changes that individual diets are unlikely to accomplish on their own. This is not a reason to give up on plant-based eating -- in fact, I highly recommend it. Although this isn’t the diet for everyone, even occasional plantbased eating can add concrete benefits to anyone’s life. Vegans are often portrayed as out of touch, preachy, and difficult to please. While these characteristics are true of certain people, it isn’t true for the vegan community as a whole. Although numbers are hard to come by, it is often estimated that 5% of Americans eat a vegetarian diet, and some smaller portion of that eschew all eggs and dairy to eat a completely plant-based diet. That means there are millions of vegans walking among us. People have many different reasons for trying plant-based eating. Some religions, such as Buddhism, promote vegetarianism, and numerous countries, primarily in Africa and Asia, have very plant heavy diets. In India, where over 80% of the population practices Hinduism or Jainism, vegetarianism is the norm. Ethiopia boasts delicious vegetarian fare, including injera bread (a personal favorite of mine). Living in America, vegetarianism is less widespread, but there are vegetarian-friendly areas. California and the West Coast as a whole are largely vegan friendly, which can probably be linked to the history of social movements, large supply of fruits and vegetables, and varied cultures that have taken root here. Speaking from first hand experience, everywhere from supermarkets to farmer’s markets offer vegan wares in abundance that would have seemed ludicrous 5-10 years ago. Despite the growing acceptance of vegetarian diets, there is still a deeply entrenched resistance to trying plant-based foods. People have a range of reasons why they are skeptical: “Where would I get my protein?” “I wouldn’t know what recipes to make.” “It seems hard to eat out.” Vegetarianism, like running or learning the flute, can be intimidating, but rewarding. There are hundreds of blogs, social media accounts, Youtube channels, and physical cookbooks you can turn to start putting together recipes. There has never been a better time in the US to try a different diet. Here are a few tips that I humbly offer as a way to attempt something new: • Start small. Try eating one meal a day without meat and see how you feel. Switching to a new style of eating is a gradual effort. Nobody expects you to ditch all meat in a day. Avoid substitutes. I personally try to avoid plant products that fake meat. Make meals that embrace vegetables instead of emulating meat products. Don’t limit yourself to just veggie burgers, veggie dogs, or fake crab cakes. There is a wide world of vegetarian dishes that just focus on vegetables. You may find your new favorite recipe. Try something new. Never had indian food? Give it a shot. Use this as a learning experience and a chance to talk to new people about foods you don’t know much about. Meal plan. it’s easier to make changes when you have a plan. Go to the store with a shopping list; it’s easier to stick to vegetables. The internet is your friend-- there are so many resources out there. Google “how to vegetarian” and do some reading. There are schedules, options for recipes, and groups you can join. Finally, make sure you know why you want to try it. Some of the main reasons people attempt it are for health reasons, to lose weight, or just try and add some variety to their diet. Don’t let plant-based eating be something you dread – approach it as a fun thing to add to post-pandemic life. articles.text: Dear Jim: We are about to start a remodel and are debating about whether to hire a designer and then a contractor, or whether we should do design-build with a single firm. Your thoughts? –Austin H. Know yourself A decision about how you want the design aspects of your project to occur should be made and stuck to. Will you be hands-on, making the bulk of the selections and design decisions? Or will you want the contractor or designer to make choices and provide you with selections to choose from? This may seem simple, but in our experience the matter of how you want to work is decided early on to avoid mistakes. Know your designer Finding and sourcing compatible fixtures, cabinets, tile, flooring, paint colors, etc. are all skills that most designers possess. However, some lack the construction knowledge needed to integrate their choices into architectural drawings and construction work. In a recent project, our client’s designer didn’t read our architect’s drawing properly Installing a narrow tub and vanity improved the space in this bathroom. Recessing appliances and closets into the crawlspace of this basement second unit created much needed working space. and ordered a vanity that was too wide, had to be returned, and reordered, causing project delays and high return shipping and restocking fees. Get to know your project First, decide on your level of involvement. Often clients tell us they are hands-off, then change their minds and want to be more involved later in the game. Understand that any changes in the design-build process, including increasing your involvement can significantly affect timelines, budget and choices. Next, make sure your contractor or design-builder has clear expectations on the decision-making process for items being selected and ordered, and the time frames for delivery and budget. Keep in mind that the current supply chains are erratic. Having to return and reorder supplies may sideline a project. Finally, in addition to your designer and contractor being a good fit for you, be sure your selections properly fit the space and are reviewed by the contractor, designer and you before being ordered. Measure twice and cut once applies to the design process, too. On display currently is “You Are Here: California Stories on the Map,” which opened just before the pandemic shuttered the museum in March 2020. The exhibit showcases a diverse range of maps from the East Bay, the entire Bay Area, and the state. It focuses on environmental surroundings, health conditions, community perspectives and creative artworks, weaved together to display the importance of location and cartography.
